title: Exam Technique & Timed Practice
content_html:
The Paper in Numbers

Everything in this lesson comes from three figures. The poetry and Shakespeare paper is two hours long, worth 80 marks, and taken closed text — no anthology, no play, nothing on the desk. Eighty marks in a hundred and twenty minutes gives you exactly one and a half minutes per mark, and every timing below is that figure applied.

Key Fact

The paper is two hours long and worth eighty marks. Forty marks go to the poetry section and forty to the Shakespeare section, so each deserves an even hour. Inside the poetry hour, part (a) and part (b) are worth twenty marks each — so they deserve thirty minutes each, planning included.

The Poetry Hour, Minute by Minute

0–5 min

Read the task, then both poems

Task first so you know the theme. Then read the anthology poem and the unseen poem, annotating only against that theme.

5–8 min

Fill the comparison grid

Idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — two columns, short quotations only.

8–30 min

Write part (a)

A comparative thesis, then three or four interwoven paragraphs. Both poems in every paragraph.

30–34 min

Choose and plan part (b)

Pick a different poem from your cluster and write your thesis sentence before you start.

34–58 min

Write part (b)

Detailed exploration of that single poem. No comparison.

58–60 min

Check and move on

Check quotations, then leave for the Shakespeare section on the hour whatever state the answer is in.

Key Fact

Part (b) is the most commonly rushed answer on this paper. Examiners report that responses are often brief, as if timing had been forgotten under pressure. It carries exactly the same twenty marks as the comparison. A thin part (b) costs as much as a thin part (a), and it is the easier of the two to fix.

Rubric Mistakes That Cost Whole Answers

A rubric infringement is a failure to read the instructions rather than a failure of skill, and it caps an answer that might otherwise have scored well. These four are the ones examiners see every year.

Answering on only one poem in part (a). The comparison must cover the anthology poem and the unseen poem together.

Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster, or one that has been removed from the current anthology. Check your cluster list before the exam, not during it.

Re-using the part (a) anthology poem in part (b). The task asks for one other poem, so the part (a) poem cannot be used again.

Comparing in part (b). No comparison is required there, and it steals the time you need for close analysis of one text.

What a Strong Answer Looks Like on the Page

Length does not earn marks. Examiners report very long scripts — some running to fifteen sides or more — whose quality suffered from their length, with the same point restated through one quotation after another. Three or four developed, interwoven paragraphs beat eight thin ones.

Keep quotations embedded and short. Four well-placed words prove more than a copied-out stanza, and they leave room for the analysis that actually earns the mark.

Two Practical Points About the Booklet

Spelling, punctuation and grammar are not assessed in the poetry section, so do not spend your final minutes proofreading. Legibility is a different matter: examiners regularly report scripts they struggle to decipher even when magnified. A mark cannot be given for a word that cannot be read.

Label your answers clearly as part (a) and part (b), and start part (b) on a fresh page. It costs nothing and it removes any doubt about which poem belongs to which task.

Week one. Untimed. Take an unfamiliar short poem, spend fifteen minutes filling a comparison grid against a cluster poem, and write nothing else. Grid practice is the highest-value drill there is.

Week two. Thirty minutes for part (a) alone, twice. Mark yourself on one question only: does every paragraph contain both poems?

Week three. Thirty minutes for part (b) alone, twice, on different cluster poems. Check your quotations against the text afterwards and count the misquotations.

Week four. The full poetry hour, both parts, in one sitting, twice. This is the only drill that tests whether you can stop part (a) on time.

The Final Check

Before you turn the page: does part (a) discuss both poems in every paragraph? Does part (b) cover a different poem from your own cluster, without comparison? Have you explained the effect of every method you named? If all three answers are yes, the answer is doing what the mark scheme asks.
exam_tip_html: Set a hard stop for part (a) at the thirty-minute mark and obey it. Almost every student who runs short on this paper does so because the comparison felt like it was going well. The marks you lose in a rushed part (b) are worth more than the marks you gain from a fourth comparison paragraph.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Two hours, eighty marks, closed text: one and a half minutes per mark, an hour for the poetry section, thirty minutes for each twenty-mark part.
  • Part (b) carries the same marks as the comparison and is the answer most often rushed.
  • Three or four developed interwoven paragraphs beat eight thin ones; length alone earns no marks.

practice_questions.text: In exactly 30 minutes: compare how these poems present a difficult decision. Stop when the time is up, whether or not you have finished. [In the exam, both poems are printed for you.]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, interwoven comparison of both poems with precise, embedded quotations and confident analysis of the effects of language, form and structure.
Secure: Clear comparison of both poems throughout, with relevant quotations and explained analysis of method.
Developing: Some comparison, often poem by poem, with supported comments on obvious techniques.
Emerging: Simple comments on one or both poems; comparison and textual support are limited or missing.

practice_questions.text: In exactly 30 minutes: explore in detail one other poem from your anthology cluster which presents an unwelcome truth. Write from memory, without your anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Convincing personal argument about the poem, precisely quoted from memory, with sophisticated analysis of the poet's methods.
Secure: Clear personal argument with accurate quotations and explained analysis of language, form or structure.
Developing: Some understanding of the poem with basic support; analysis of method is limited.
Emerging: Simple comments on the poem; quotations are absent, vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Complete the full poetry hour in one sitting. Part (a): compare how these poems present the effect of the past on the present. [In the exam, both poems are printed for you.]
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, interwoven comparison of both poems with precise, embedded quotations and confident analysis of the effects of language, form and structure.
Secure: Clear comparison of both poems throughout, with relevant quotations and explained analysis of method.
Developing: Some comparison, often poem by poem, with supported comments on obvious techniques.
Emerging: Simple comments on one or both poems; comparison and textual support are limited or missing.

practice_questions.text: Complete the full poetry hour in one sitting. Part (b): explore in detail one other poem from your cluster which presents an experience the speaker cannot share.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Convincing personal argument about the poem, precisely quoted from memory, with sophisticated analysis of the poet's methods.
Secure: Clear personal argument with accurate quotations and explained analysis of language, form or structure.
Developing: Some understanding of the poem with basic support; analysis of method is limited.
Emerging: Simple comments on the poem; quotations are absent, vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Spend only 5 minutes planning, then 25 minutes writing: compare how these poems present anger. Judge your answer solely on whether both poems appear in every paragraph. [In the exam, both poems are printed for you.]
practice_questions.marks:

Secure: Clear comparison of both poems throughout, with relevant quotations and explained analysis of method.
Developing: Some comparison, often poem by poem, with supported comments on obvious techniques.
Emerging: Simple comments on one or both poems; comparison and textual support are limited or missing.

practice_questions.text: In exactly 30 minutes: explore in detail one other poem from your anthology cluster which presents hope. Afterwards, check every quotation against the text and count your misquotations.
